title: Koan Practice
speaker: Burai Rick Spencer
summary: Burai Rick Spencer shares their personal experience with koan practice, highlighting the importance of letting go of conceptual thinking and ego-based perspectives in order to truly understand a koan like "Mu." Through their own struggles and eventual breakthroughs, they illustrate that the goal of koan study is not to arrive at a definitive answer, but rather to transcend conceptual boundaries and experience reality directly. By doing so, one can see the world as an interconnected whole, where our individual sense of self dissolves into the vastness of existence.

sentences.text: Good evening.
I really should begin by apologizing for not being here last week when I was scheduled to be here, but I'm sure you had a wonderful time without me, so maybe this will be a letdown after last week.
But I did make the bus today.
Those of you who don't know me, there are some faces that are unfamiliar.
My name is Rick Spencer, or Burai Rick Spencer to use my dharma name.
I'm a Zen priest, a student of Norman Fischer, as is Tim.
I began Zen practice in Vancouver, but right now I live in Mexico.
I've been in Mexico for five years now.
What's the right word?
I'm practicing with a small group of Mexicans and students in Puerto Vallarta.
But I'm visiting Vancouver.
Well, I'm visiting Bellingham right now, but I'm visiting Vancouver for a time and Tim invited me to come down and give a talk.
I said yes and then missed the bus, but here I am again.
I wanted to talk about a koan this evening.
To begin with, I think I'll say just a little bit about my experience of koan practice.
I suspect that most of us have at least heard of these old Zen anecdotes called koans.
They seem to be one of the things we hear about the most.
In fact, I think it's coming into the vernacular almost like Zen is, so that there will be Zen beauty salons or MP3 players.
I'm not sure exactly where koans fit in that, but I think they're coming in as well.
Like probably many or most of you, I'd already heard of koan practice before I actually met my first Zen teacher.
My first teacher was a Rinzai teacher.
He assigned koans to his students.
I knew this much before I met him.
I began sitting with a group of his students before I actually met the teacher.
I knew there were koans, but nobody ever talked about them.
It seemed to be kind of a forbidden topic.
Well, I assumed that he would assign me one of the well-known traditional Zen koans from one of the koan collections that I'd read about.
Most of the books that I'd read said that usually the first koan is Mu, or Jiaozhuo's dog.
A monk asked Jiaozhuo, does a dog have buddha nature?
Jiaozhuo answers, "Mu," or "without."
Well, I didn't think about that.
I decided that when I went in and he assigned me that koan, I would say that it's a mistake to say that a dog has buddha nature, because this buddha nature isn't separate from the dog.
A dog is buddha nature.
Buddha nature shouldn't be considered something that's separate.
Well, I never got the chance.
He assigned something completely different.
As a first koan, he said, "How do you realize yourself when you hear this sound?"
And then he hit the floor with a stick.
How do you realize yourself when you hear a sound?
I had absolutely no idea what he meant, what he was asking, or how I should respond.
In sesshin, in a retreat, each student would go to see the roshi four times a day to present their understanding of their koan.
Time after time, I went back to see him and he would say, "How do you realize yourself when you hear this sound?"
And I would try to think of something to say.
"The sound goes right through."
He'd laugh.
He'd ring his bell.
Send me off.
The whole thing usually took a little bit less than a minute.
One time I asked him how I could use my zazen to find the answer to my koan.
He didn't say a word.
I asked him how he could use his zazen.
He just brought himself up into a straight, formal zazen posture.
He breathed in, breathed out, and then he rang his bell.
He sent me out.
It was really a very, very clear answer, but I did not understand that clear answer at the time.
It wasn't at all clear to me.
I had read, and I read a lot, in some Zen books that sometimes a teacher or a student would shout or slap the floor or do some demonstrative action to present an understanding of a koan.
So I thought I'd give that a try.
No luck.
So then I decided maybe I should be a little bit more daring.
I plotted: the next time I go in, when he lifts up his stick and he's ready to strike the floor, I'm going to grab that stick out of his hand and I'm going to strike the floor.
That will show him.
So I did.
I actually summoned up the courage and managed to snatch it away from him.
I hit the floor and he said, "Oh, not that sound, this sound.
Not that sound, this sound."
I felt like he'd pulled the rug out from under me.
He rang his bell.
I stumbled out.
Well, I kept going back and he kept ringing me out.
Eventually, I just stopped trying so hard and I just kept going in to spend some time with him, just to see what might happen.
Once in a while, he'd tap out a little rhythm with his stick and I just began to accompany him or tap out a counter rhythm or just make some sort of music together.
I hadn't really given up, but I had let go of a lot of my intensity and the pressure that I put on myself to succeed, to win.
I really stopped planning what I would do the next time I saw him.
After a while, he gave me another koan.
I still don't know if he was satisfied with my response or he thought that was too hard for me, better give me something else.
Or maybe he was just a little tired and for his own entertainment he thought he would give me something else to enjoy, whatever show I might attempt.
Well, this was nothing at all like the koan experiences that I read about in books.
I never felt any kind of spectacular breakthrough.
The koans themselves were never the curious stories about ancient Zen worthies.
After several years with this teacher, I left.
Troubling things had been happening in the community and at first I hoped to be a part of a healing process, but eventually I lost confidence that healing would take place.
Eventually I went to study with Robert Aitken Roshi, one of the first Western Zen teachers and someone who assigned the koan Mu, Xiaozhou's dog, to his beginning students.

In our first meeting together, when I talked a little bit about my history, we decided together that it would be best if I didn't start working on a koan with him, that I would just do quiet sitting, shikantaza.
That would be our practice together.
Then maybe at some later time he felt that it might be appropriate to assign the koan to me.
Then a few days later in that same sesshin, after several interviews, he suggested that it would be a good idea to start working on the koan Mu.
I said I'd rather not.
I felt like I was really connecting to something through just going in to see him and silently sitting shikantaza.
I didn't feel the urge, the desire or the need to start studying a koan.
This is my disclaimer before I start talking about this koan: when it comes to koan practice, I am a dropout and a failure.
In some traditions, a student will take up a single koan and practice with that koan for the rest of their life.
Martine Batchelor describes her Korean Zen teacher, who practiced with the koan "What is this?" for his entire life.
He never exhausted its value.

Some other Korean teachers have relied on a curriculum of koans passing from one to another to another, as do most teachers in the Japanese Rinzai tradition and in the Sanbo Kyodan, the Three Treasures tradition.
For many of them, Zhao Zhuo's Mu is the beginning of koan study.
In his commentary on this koan, Muma says that we should take the koan up like a red hot iron ball.
You try to vomit it out, but you can't.
We really don't know from the ancient texts in what way Zen students advanced from koan to koan under the guidance of a teacher.
How is it that they practiced koans with their teacher?
We really don't know.
The koan system that seems to be pretty much in standard use today was developed in the 18th century by Hakuen, a Japanese Rinzai teacher.
Typically, a student comes into the interview room to manifest or to present some kind of action or response inspired by the koan.
It's not an explanation of the meaning of the koan or some analysis.

Typically, for the koan Mu, it seems that the student might manifest the word itself, Mu, being spoken, but most students already know this, so it's not just coming in and speaking or singing or shouting or whispering "Mu."
It's presenting Mu in such a way that the teacher can see that the student has clearly cut off conceptual thinking and become one with the activity of the koan.
One time, I remember, I went in to present my understanding of a koan to my old teacher and I felt very free and very confident somehow when I went in and responded.
I could see that he was pleased, content, satisfied with the koan.
I could see that he was satisfied perhaps with what I was doing.
Just at the end of this moment, I kind of looked at him for his approval and he could tell that right in that instant my ego had inserted itself.
I wanted him to say "good boy" or something like that, so he shook his head and rang his bell and there I went.

In the book of Soko Morinaga Roshi, a more or less contemporary Japanese Rinzai teacher, in talking about practicing koans with his students, he said, "What I am eagerly awaiting in the consultation room is for someone to come in possessed by an irrepressible joy.
I am not looking for an answer to a koan."
Well, my first teacher in a sesshin would choose a single koan for the subject of all of his dharma talks and every day for seven days he would present another talk about that particular koan.
He never ran out of things to say.
There was always something worthwhile and he really never could have finished everything that there might have been to say.
The fact that I am going to start talking about a koan in a minute, I might have some things to say.
They might agree with what other people have said or not.
Don't expect me to clear anything up.
I think at best maybe this could be like a walk through the woods.
There is always something new to discover on the trail.
The day changes, the weather, the season.
It is the same trail and yet it is never the same trail.
The koan that I decided I wanted to talk about is mostly for the season.
It is not because I think I have something important to say or that there is some important thing I understand.
It is mostly the season that just brought this up for me.
It seems to me very close in this season, in the fall.
This is from the Blue Cliff Record, case number 53.
*Once when Great Master Ma and Bai Zhang were walking together, they saw some wild ducks fly by.
The great master asked, what was that?
Zhang said, wild ducks.
The great master said, where have they gone?
Zhang said, they have flown away.
The great master then twisted Bai Zhang's nose.
Zhang cried out in pain and the great master said, when have they ever flown away?*
Well, this is my fall koan.
I am guessing that at one time or another all of us have seen wild ducks or geese flying by.
It is quite amazing how fast they fly.
When they are high in the sky it is hard to get a sense really of how fast they are flying.
But I looked it up on the internet and when they are nearer to the ground you can really feel that speed.
They seem to whiz by like cars on the highway and they fly just as fast as cars on the highway, anywhere between 60 to 100 kilometers per hour.
I think that is like 40 to 60 miles per hour more or less for you people.
So when you are outside and a group of low flying ducks speeds past, it feels like they come out of nowhere and then disappear so quickly.
You might wonder if they were really there.
Well, maybe that is what it was like when Bai Zhang and Matsu were out walking.
Some low flying ducks shot past and then disappeared.
And maybe that was what prompted this little dialogue, or little anecdote.
Master Ma in this koan is Matsu, who was one of the greats of the Zen tradition.
He lived from the year 709 to 788, and among his over 100 successors were Bai Zhang and Nanquan, both of whom figure very prominently in the koan literature.
Matsu was said to be very powerful physically.
One description of him said he strode like an ox and glared like a tiger.
His extended tongue covered his nose.
I think in those days if you said that somebody had a very long tongue, it meant that they were very eloquent, that they used words with great skill.
I don't know.
Matsu's teaching style was also very dramatic.
He was known for sudden surprising actions like shouting, or striking a student with a stick, or grabbing a student by the nose, as he does with Bai Zhang.
Bai Zhang seems to have been a very practical and down to earth teacher.
As a young man he studied the rules of classical Buddhism before he became a student of Matsu.
Later, when he became an independent teacher in his own monastery, he is credited with formulating a whole new set of rules and regulations for monastic practice.
Bai Zhang put great emphasis on work as an important practice in the monastery.
There were practical necessities for work practice, since Zen monasteries kept themselves away from the support of royal patronage.
But it was more than just a necessity.
Zen made a positive choice out of this necessity.
Even today this is something that distinguishes the Zen school.
You could say that in Zen the practical result of work is less important than the spiritual aspect of it.
Work is a form of meditation.
Having food to eat or a clean place to practice is a by-product.
You could almost say that this is true, but not quite.
The by-product, food, heat, cleanliness, order, etc., really shouldn't be separated.
It's no less spiritual than the awareness that is cultivated through meditation.
Cultivating awareness, wisdom, and compassion depends on forms and details in order to be made manifest.
There is no awakening without its expression.
Perhaps Bai Zhang's practice was to emphasize practical details of form just to balance the emphasis on emptiness that came from the meditation hall.
Complete practice includes both sitting down and getting up, both dissolving the self in union with all things, and fully manifesting the form of just one moment of existence.
At first it might look as though one practice emphasizes form and another practice emphasizes emptiness, and that both of these emphases exist in a kind of balance.
Not too much of this, not too much of that, just enough of each.
I would say that maybe that's a good start, but it's only a start.
If we look at it that way, there's a kind of tension between form and emptiness.
I think the true emphasis found in both practices is harmony, not tension.
There aren't two things in balance.
There's one thing.
What is it?
But I'm getting ahead of myself.
So let's go back to Bai Zhang and Matsu.
They're walking, and suddenly some ducks whiz past, and Matsu sees a teaching opportunity.
What was that?
For Matsu, ducks suddenly appearing and disappearing is nothing other than Buddha nature expressing itself.
Bai Zhang quite sincerely answers his teacher's question: wild ducks.
Straight, clear, to the point.
Seems a good answer.
But Matsu has not exhausted yet this opportunity to teach.
Where have they gone? he asks.
They've flown away.
Another answer that is simple and clear and to the point.
Both of Bai Zhang's responses have been expressions of relative truth.
Just what is this thing that is arising at this moment?
Matsu knows that this is a good answer, and just because it's a good answer, he sees the opportunity to push Bai Zhang just a little further.
Bai Zhang is standing firmly on solid ground, and Matsu helps him to see that this solid ground is just on the edge of a cliff.
Matsu very kindly pushes Bai Zhang off the cliff.
When have they ever flown away?
Another way that we might look at Bai Zhang's answers is to understand that he said, wild ducks were here, now they're not here.
But Matsu's response and nose-twisting is of a very different order.
I think that he is asking, what is this here?
How can we say this is here, and that is not here?
When I was 13, my family moved from suburban Philadelphia to a small town in South Dakota.
So now you know that not only am I Canadian and Mexican, I'm a former American too.
Part of what is known as the Great Plains.
We moved in the fall from one of the most densely populated parts of the U.S. to one of the most sparsely populated parts.
I remember in those first few months waking up from a sound sleep late one night at the sound of geese.
It seemed that there were hundreds of geese flying overhead, and their calls were so loud that they woke me up.
This was something I'd never heard before, but it was only the beginning.
It wasn't just a few geese or a few hundred geese.
There's really no way to say how many geese there were.
The loud calling of geese flying overhead continued for several hours, and I barely slept the rest of that night.
This was just one of several nights that fall when the enormous migration of geese could only be measured by hours and not by numbers.
I found that a little frightening.

I think it was the first time that I'd ever felt so strongly the presence of nature expressed in such a way: the existence of something so much larger and so much more active than anything else that I'd ever seen before.
It made me feel a little smaller and a little less safe and a little less secure in our little wooden house.
It's been many years since I lived in the plains, and I hope that this still happens.
I fear that maybe not as many hours as before, but I hope that people still have that experience.
Many years later, I remember talking with a friend in Vancouver, and he told me of one of the things that he did to deal with moments when his worries and his concerns began to overwhelm him.
He said, I try to think of a great whale swimming way out in the middle of the ocean, thousands of kilometers away from here.
What seems so important to me doesn't matter at all to that whale, and that helps me to put things in perspective.
That reminds me of another oddly similar story, a saying of Tug McGraw, who was a baseball pitcher in the 70s.
He said, 10 million years from now when the sun burns out and the earth is just a frozen snowball hurtling through space, nobody's going to care whether or not I got this guy out.
So we can fool ourselves with our sense of here and now, and we can start to think that it's all about us.
That's maybe not the right sentence.
I start to think that it's all about me.
You start to think it's all about you.
Here and now is me, me, me.
What's in this for me?
How will this affect my situation?
What advantage is in this for me?
I am the greatest, the smartest, the coolest, the best person in the world.
Why is this happening to me?
I'm such a failure.
Nobody loves me.
Good or bad, it's all about me.
I'm the only person here who counts.
Others are here only insofar as they have an effect on me.
Well, when that's our attitude, all the harmony has gone out of our life.
Our sense of here becomes a prison.
But in this prison, we are the prisoners and the jailers.
We ourselves can open the door.
Here ceases to be a prison when we can see the door.
Here is a prison when we're clinging to the illusion of me against the world.
That illusion cannot pass through the door.
When we let go of that illusion, here is a wide open door.
This place, this moment is a point of entry into the infinite.
When have they ever flown away?
According to the record, a painful twist to the nose along with this response brought Bai Jiang to great realization, and the story continues.
The next day, Matsu entered the hall to give a talk.
But Bai Jiang entered and rolled up the bowing mat before Matsu could make his formal bows.
Matsu just got up and left.
And later he asked Bai Jiang, why did you roll up the bowing mat before I could speak?
Bai Jiang said, yesterday you twisted my nose and it hurt.
Matsu said, where in your mind do you keep yesterday's matter?
Bai Jiang said, the nose does not hurt today.
Matsu said, you understand today's matter very well.
So you might think this sounds like a story about how Bai Jiang got even with Matsu.
But I don't think that's quite it.
Bai Jiang and Matsu were playing with each other.
There is intimacy and there is trust in their actions.
And even though you might say that Matsu taught Bai Jiang a lesson, he did so with great confidence in Bai Jiang's awakened nature.
And I think that Bai Jiang running off with a bowing mat is more like a game of tag than anything else.
So after this last conversation, Bai Jiang left crying.
Another monk asked him, why are you crying?
And Bai Jiang said, you'll have to go and ask the master.
So the monk went to ask Matsu why Bai Jiang was crying, and Matsu said, you'll have to ask Bai Jiang.
So the poor monk returned to find Bai Jiang laughing.
And he said, a minute ago you were crying, now you're laughing.
Please explain.
Bai Jiang replied, I was crying before, now I'm laughing.
So all of this, I think, is a wonderful little short work of Zen theater.
First there's a scene where Matsu shows Bai Jiang that here includes the entire universe.
There's nothing that is outside of here.
How could anything fly away?
With a painful twist of his nose, Bai Jiang enters the realm of absolute truth through the doorway of one momentary event.
Then in act two, Bai Jiang removes Matsu's bowing mat.
He steals the location away before the event can take place.
Is there another doorway?
Is there any meaning in Matsu's leaving?
Then we come to act three and audience participation.
Matsu and Bai Jiang have enjoyed playing together so much that their enthusiasm draws more people into the teaching.
So I could ask you if Bai Jiang's crying and his laughing are examples of the relative or of the absolute.
I could ask you if a doorway is an entrance or an exit.
Does it have to be either?
Thank you for listening.
That's my talk.

It is mostly the season that just brought this up for me. It seems to me very close in this season, in the fall. This is from the Blue Cliff Record, case number 53. Once when great masterminds and Bai Zhang were walking together, they saw some wild ducks fly by. The great master asked, what was that? Zhang said, wild ducks. The great master said, where have they gone? Zhang said, they have flown away.

The great master then twisted Bai Zhang's nose. Zhang cried out in pain and the great master said, when have they ever flown away? Well, this is my fall koan. I am guessing that at one time or another all of us have seen wild ducks or geese flying by. It is quite amazing how fast they fly. When they are high in the sky it is hard to get a sense really of how fast they are flying. But I looked it up on the internet and when they are nearer to the ground you can really feel that speed. They seem to whiz by like cars on the highway and they fly just as fast as cars on the highway, anywhere between 60 to 100 kilometers per hour. I think that is like 40 to 60 miles per hour

more or less for you people. So when you are outside and a group of low flying ducks speeds past, it feels like they come out of nowhere and then disappear so quickly. You might wonder if they were really there. Well maybe that is what it was like when Bai Zhang and Matsu were out walking. Some low flying ducks shot past and then disappeared. And maybe that was what prompted this little dialogue or little anecdote. Master Ma in this koan is Matsu who was one of the greats of the Zen tradition. He lived from the year 709 to 788 and among his over 100 successors were Bai Zhang and Nanquan, both of whom figure very prominently in the koan literature.

Matsu was said to be very powerful physically. One description of him said he strode like an ox and glared like a tiger. His extended tongue covered his nose. I think in those days if you said that somebody had a very long tongue, it meant that they were very eloquent, that they used words with great skill. I don't know. Matsu's teaching style was also very dramatic. He was known for sudden surprising actions like shouting or striking a student with a stick or grabbing a student by the nose as he does with Bai Zhang. Bai Zhang seems to have been a very practical and down to earth teacher.

As a young man he studied the rules of classical Buddhism before he became a student of Matsu. Later, when he became an independent teacher in his own monastery, he is credited with formulating a whole new set of rules and regulations for monastic practice. Bai Zhang put great emphasis on work as an important practice in the monastery. There were practical necessities for work practice since Zen monasteries kept themselves away from the support of royal patronage. But it was more than just a necessity. Zen made a positive choice out of this necessity. Even today this is something that distinguishes the Zen school. You could say that in Zen

the practical result of work is less important than the spiritual aspect of it. Work is a form of meditation. Having food to eat or a clean place to practice is a by-product. You could almost say that this is true, but not quite. The by-product, food, heat, cleanliness, order, etc., really shouldn't be separated. It's no less spiritual than the awareness that is cultivated through meditation. Cultivating awareness, wisdom, and compassion depends on forms and details in order to be made manifest. There is no awakening without its expression. Perhaps Bai Zhang's practice was to emphasize practical details of form just to balance the emphasis on emptiness that came from

the meditation hall. Complete practice includes both sitting down and getting up, both dissolving the self in union with all things, and fully manifesting the form of just one moment of existence. At first it might look as though one practice emphasizes form and another practice emphasizes emptiness, and that both of these emphases exist in a kind of balance. Not too much of this, not too much of that, just enough of each. I would say that maybe that's a good start, but it's only a start. If we look at it that way, there's a kind of tension between form and emptiness. I think the true emphasis found in both practices is harmony, not tension. There aren't two things in balance. There's one thing. What

is it? But I'm getting ahead of myself. So let's go back to Bai Zhang and Matsu. They're walking, and suddenly some duck's whiz passed, and Matsu sees a teaching opportunity. What was that? For Matsu, ducks suddenly appearing and disappearing is nothing other than Buddha nature expressing itself. Bai Zhang quite sincerely answers his teacher's question. Wild ducks. Straight, clear, to the point. Seems a good answer. But Matsu has not exhausted yet this opportunity to teach. Where have they gone? He asks. They've flown away. Another answer that is simple and clear and to the point. Both of Bai Zhang's responses have been expressions of relative truth. Just what is this thing that is arising at

this moment? Matsu knows that this is a good answer, and just because it's a good answer, he sees the opportunity to push Bai Zhang just a little further. Bai Zhang is standing firmly on solid ground, and Matsu helps him to see that this solid ground is just on the edge of a cliff. Matsu very kindly pushes Bai Zhang off the cliff. When have they ever flown away? Another way that we might look at Bai Zhang's answers is to understand that he said, wild ducks were here, now they're not here. But Matsu's response and nose-twisting is a very different order. I think that he is asking, what is this here? How can we say this is here, and that is not here?

When I was 13, my family moved from suburban Philadelphia to a small town in South Dakota. So now you know that not only am I Canadian and Mexican, I'm a former American too. Part of what is known as the Great Plains. We moved in the fall from one of the most densely populated parts of the U.S. to one of the most sparsely populated parts. I remember in those first few months waking up from a sound sleep late one night at the sound of geese. It seemed that there were hundreds of geese flying overhead and their calls were so loud that they woke me up. This was something I'd never heard before, but it was only the beginning. It wasn't just a few geese or a few hundred

geese. There's really no way to say how many geese there were. The loud calling of geese flying overhead continued for several hours, and I barely slept the rest of that night. This was just one of several nights that fall when the enormous migration of geese could only be measured by hours and not by numbers. I found that a little frightening. I think it was the first time that I'd ever felt so strongly the presence of nature expressed in such a way. The existence of something so much larger and so much more active than anything else that I'd ever seen before. It made me feel a little smaller and a little less safe and a little less secure in our

little wooden house. It's been many years since I lived in the plains, and I hope that this still happens. I fear that maybe not as many hours as before, but I hope that people still have that experience. Many years later, I remember talking with a friend in Vancouver, and he told me of one of the things that he did to deal with moments when his worries and his concerns began to overwhelm him. He said, I try to think of a great whale swimming way out in the middle of the ocean, thousands of kilometers away from here. What seems so important to me doesn't matter at all to that whale, and that helps me to put things in perspective.

That reminds me of another oddly similar story, a saying of Tug McGraw, who was a baseball pitcher in the 70s. He said, 10 million years from now when the sun burns out and the earth is just a frozen snowball hurtling through space, nobody's going to care whether or not I got this guy out. So we can fool ourselves with our sense of here and now, and we can start to think that it's all about us. That's maybe not the right sentence. I start to think that it's all about me. You start to think it's all about you. Here and now is me, me, me. What's in this for me? How will this affect my situation? What advantage is in this for me? I am the greatest,

the smartest, the coolest, the best person in the world. Why is this happening to me? I'm such a failure. Nobody loves me. Good or bad, it's all about me. I'm the only person here who counts. Others are here only insofar as they have an effect on me. Well, when that's our attitude, all the harmony has gone out of our life. Our sense of here becomes a prison. But in this prison, we are the prisoners and the jailers. We ourselves can open the door. Here ceases to be a prison when we can see the door. Here is a prison when we're clinging to the illusion of me against the world. That illusion cannot pass through the door. When we let go of that illusion, here is a wide open

door. This place, this moment is a point of entry into the infinite. When have they ever flown away? According to the record, a painful twist to the nose along with this response brought Bai Jiang to great realization and the story continues. The next day, Matsu entered the hall to give a talk. But Bai Jiang entered and rolled up the bowing mat before Matsu could make his formal bows. Matsu just got up and left. And later he asked Bai Jiang, why did you roll up the bowing mat before I could speak? Bai Jiang said, yesterday you twisted my nose and it hurt. Matsu said, where in your mind do you keep yesterday's matter? Bai Jiang said, the nose does not hurt today. Matsu said,

you understand today's matter very well. So you might think this sounds like a story about how Bai Jiang got even with Matsu. But I don't think that's quite it. Bai Jiang and Matsu were playing with each other. There is intimacy and there is trust in their actions. And even though you might say that Matsu taught Bai Jiang a lesson, he did so with great confidence in Bai Jiang's awakened nature. And I think that Bai Jiang running off with a bowing mat is more like a game of tag than anything else. So after this last conversation, Bai Jiang left crying. Another monk asked him, why are you crying? And Bai Jiang said, you'll have to go and ask the master. So the monk went

to ask Matsu why Bai Jiang was crying and Matsu said, you'll have to ask Bai Jiang. So the poor monk returned to find Bai Jiang laughing. And he said, a minute ago you were crying, now you're laughing. Please explain. Bai Jiang replied, I was crying before, now I'm laughing. So all of this I think is a wonderful little short work of Zen theater. First there's a scene where Matsu shows Bai Jiang that here includes the entire universe. There's nothing that is outside of here. How could anything fly away? With a painful twist of his nose, Bai Jiang enters the realm of absolute truth through the doorway of one momentary event. Then in act two, Bai Jiang removes Matsu's bowing

mat. He steals the location away before the event can take place. Is there another doorway? Is there any meaning in Matsu's leaving? Then we come to act three and audience participation. Matsu and Bai Jiang have enjoyed playing together so much that their enthusiasm draws more people into the teaching. So I could ask you if Bai Jiang's crying and his laughing are examples of the relative or of the absolute. I could ask you if a doorway is an entrance or an exit. Does it have to be either? Thank you for listening. That's my talk.
